title: AI-authored calls for papers and the rise of the LLM leadership class
author: Stephen Vainker
summary: Vainker argues that the problem with low-quality LLM-written papers in educational research lies with BERA's leadership and editorial policies, not with AI itself. His evidence is that five current special-section calls for papers in the British Journal of Educational Technology are themselves LLM-written, the worst being one on students' AI literacy. He uses Google Scholar counts of post-2022 phrases, the absence of any citations, and a hallucinated central premise about the literature to make the case. He adds the lead author's jump in output from about two papers a year to roughly one every three weeks. From this he infers an LLM leadership class in education academia, risen through LLM writing and now shaping the field through more of it, and he criticizes the silent majority of UK academics who have said nothing.
points: The failure he identifies is editorial and institutional: basic review standards were not applied, so blaming the volume of AI submissions is a dodge.
Phrase-frequency evidence from Google Scholar, such as 'advancements in fostering' and 'offering actionable insights into', is his forensic method for showing LLM authorship.
The call's core premise, that student-centered and post-generative AI literacy research is lacking, is contradicted by papers its own authors have cited.
A sudden jump in author output from two papers a year to one every three weeks is offered as a sign that LLMs do most of the work.
He argues that academic silence enables an emerging LLM leadership class that shapes the field.
quotes: To underline the point that the problem is with BERA leadership and policies, rather than AI itself, in this post I will show that five of the current calls for papers for special sections in the British Journal of Educational Technology (BJET) are themselves LLM-written. By LLM-written I do not merely mean that they have been polished by AI, but in at least one case it has been fully generated with very little human input.

Even the title contains a clear post-LLM phrase: ‘advancements in fostering’ appears on Google Scholar only 7 times before 2022 and 217 times since, including 93 times in 2025, the year the call for papers was published. The call for papers contains no citations or references, which is extremely unhelpful given that it is supposed to provide direction to the field.

The paragraph is simply cobbled together from plausible sounding academic language. In total across the call for paper there are 38 phrases that never, or almost never appeared before 2022 but have since come into use. (see table below) That cannot be a coincidence.

Between 2014 and 2021 he wrote 16 papers, at an average of two a year, a totally normal output. In 2023 he published 13 papers, 17 papers in 2024 , and a further 17 in 2025. So suddenly, he is producing a paper every three weeks, and sustaining it for years.

The most telling phrase is ‘offering actionable insights into’, which was used only 13 times before 2022 and has been used 1,138 times since. This paragraph is not only full of post-LLM phrases (‘novel possibilities for fostering’ etc.) but also contains an LLM tell of sometimes including two authors before listing et al., and sometimes only one:

That there are five AI-generated, and often absurd, calls for papers in the BJET is alarming because it suggests the rise of an LLM leadership class in education academia. That is to say, a group of people who have risen through academia via LLM writing and now serve as thought leaders shaping the field through further LLM writing.
